chunks.title: [Master Express Lesson 5] CLO Modularization Special Live Broadcast
chunks.content: ## Interactive Voting for Software Optimization This section explains the interactive voting feature integrated into the live broadcast platform, designed to gather user feedback on software usage to optimize future versions. - A small voting window is available below the dynamic section. - The vote consists of one question aimed at understanding user needs. - Desktop users can pull down the dynamic content section to vote. - Mobile users should first shrink the screen, click the anchor, then access the dynamic section to complete the questionnaire. - The vote is anonymous, encouraging honest responses. - Results will inform improvements for software tailored to Chinese users. --- ## Introduction to CLO Modularization This section covers the rationale behind CLO’s modularization function, its primary use cases, and how it assists designers in garment creation through module management. - CLO software supports an all-around role-based approach requiring modular design handling. - Designers primarily focus on arranging and modifying garment analysis. - Modularization divides a garment into parts (e.g., collar, front, sleeve) for easy switching and combination. - This function allows designers to add sections (like pockets or cross-sections) and redesign clothing efficiently. - Example: Using a shirt model to demonstrate modular drawing and module drawing modes. --- ## Module Drawing vs. Module Drawing Change This section distinguishes between "module drawing" and "module drawing change" modes within CLO, focusing on their purposes and workflows. - **Module Drawing Change**: For frequent updates; allows changing a module and importing it into the warehouse for free assembly. - **Module Drawing Mode**: For creating new modules; includes a module editor and module drawing model presets. - Users select garment types (e.g., shirt) and model variants (e.g., basic, short sleeve) as presets. - The interface shows module frames (outer boundaries) and module structures (internal parts). --- ## Assigning Panels to Module Frames This section details the procedure for placing garment panels into their respective module frames and how the system detects seams. - Panels must be assigned to corresponding module frames (e.g., collar panel to collar frame). - Selecting a module frame highlights the matching panel with a black border. - The module frame automatically adjusts size (enlarges or shrinks) based on panel dimensions. - Sleeve panels require special attention to placement (e.g., avoid left-right mix-up). - Overlapping parts after placement can be adjusted by moving the module frame. --- ## Foundation and Sewing Line Creation This section explains foundation lines and sewing line creation between panels and modules, emphasizing correct alignment and sewing directions. - Foundation lines are created only between panel and module frame, not between panels directly. - Use the free foundation tool to connect panels with module frames. - "Knife" lines (cutting lines) must align with garment edges like the shoulder line. - Avoid using edge lines for foundation to prevent simulated bulges. - Foundation lines become dark black when completed and are color-coded for sewing. - Sewing follows foundation lines; sewing direction must be consistent (knife downward).

chunks.title: [Master Express Lesson 5] CLO Modularization Special Live Broadcast
chunks.content: - Foundation lines are created only between panel and module frame, not between panels directly. - Use the free foundation tool to connect panels with module frames. - "Knife" lines (cutting lines) must align with garment edges like the shoulder line. - Avoid using edge lines for foundation to prevent simulated bulges. - Foundation lines become dark black when completed and are color-coded for sewing. - Sewing follows foundation lines; sewing direction must be consistent (knife downward). - Incorrect sewing direction can be fixed by deleting and resewing or using the direction arrow tool. - Use the Shift key to refine sewing across multiple sections (1 to n sewing). - Sewing examples include side seams, shoulder lines, sleeve seams, and cuffs. - The system recognizes sewn sections for simulation purposes. --- ## Sewing Techniques for Sleeves This section describes detailed sleeve sewing steps, including handling overlapping parts and sewing order. - Start sewing from the long edge of the sleeve. - Skip fold parts when sewing overlapping sections. - Complete sewing by turning around and finishing at the sleeve opening. - Use Shift key for continuous sewing refinement. - Check for seam openings or incomplete seams after sewing. - Sleeves do not require sewing with the mold panel if they only seam with other panels. --- ## Module and Panel Sewing Line Display This section introduces tools for toggling module and panel sewing line visibility to assist in quality checking. - The “module sewing line display” and “panel sewing line display” tools allow switching views. - Users can choose display modes based on personal preferences during design and verification. --- ## Module Simulation and Locking This section explains how to simulate garment modules, handle locked pieces, and activate modules for editing. - Before saving a module, simulate to check seams and fit. - Locked pieces appear gray and are inactive during simulation. - To activate a piece, repeatedly click it until it unlocks. - Simulation shows default system seams and stitching behavior. - Pausing and restarting simulation helps verify sewing correctness. --- ## Creating and Saving Modules This section outlines the workflow to create, name, save, and manage garment modules within CLO. - Use the module editor interface with two icons: open and save. - Save modules by selecting target folders and naming files (e.g., "Zheng Shan"). - Module files use the extension `.ZMD2`. - Module extractors (views) can be added or switched, such as vertical perspectives. - Saved modules are organized in file folders for easy retrieval. - Modules can be combined or newly saved by importing files into the library. - Changes to modules (e.g., collars) require resewing and resaving to update files. --- ## Module Assembly and Editing This section covers how to assemble garments by combining modular parts and edit individual components. - Modules such as collars, fronts, sleeves, cuffs, and embroidery can be quickly switched by double-clicking. - Designers can delete unwanted parts from module frames to customize garment structure.

chunks.content: - Modules can be combined or newly saved by importing files into the library. - Changes to modules (e.g., collars) require resewing and resaving to update files. --- ## Module Assembly and Editing This section covers how to assemble garments by combining modular parts and edit individual components. - Modules such as collars, fronts, sleeves, cuffs, and embroidery can be quickly switched by double-clicking. - Designers can delete unwanted parts from module frames to customize garment structure. - Internal lines can be added or removed to separate garment sections. - Splitting lines into segments allows for individual piece manipulation and fabric application. - Fabric changes can be applied by selecting panels and dragging new fabric swatches. - Internal line display can be toggled off for clearer visualization. - Final garments can be simulated to preview combined modules and fabric changes. --- ## Module Conversion and Management Options This section explains module conversion options, including default system modules, adding, resetting, updating, and grouping. - CLO provides default module sets: foldable, male, and female module frames. - Double-clicking module parts allows quick switching. - Users can delete unwanted parts and manage module contents. - The "increase" button imports saved modules from folders. - "Reset" restores module sets to system defaults, removing imported files. - "Update" refreshes the module list after changes. - "Add group" allows classification, e.g., grouping different sizes to avoid simulation conflicts. - "Add module structure" supports saving new module configurations. - Finished edits are finalized by clicking the "end" button. --- ## Module Relationship and Deletion This section describes how to manage module relationships and delete module frames within the 2D window. - Right-click the blank area in the 2D window to access “delete module relationship.” - Confirm deletion to remove unwanted module frames. - Editing tools can select and delete versions or module frames as needed. --- ## Measurement and Quick Photo Extraction This section introduces extractors for module measurement and quick photo capture to preview module designs. - Extractors provide different views (e.g., vertical perspective) for measuring modules. - Quick photos capture module previews for use in documentation or presentations. - Extractor images are added to module files for reference. --- ## Material Hardness Adjustment This section explains how to adjust material properties to affect garment hardness and bending strength. - Material hardness can be modified via parameters such as the "gold tail sand" line adjusted to 99. - Adjusting this parameter increases material stiffness. - Designers can create belt adjustment codes by drawing internal lines and adding rendering thickness. - Thickness values (e.g., 5 units) and curve adjustments control bulge and rigidity. - This technique allows creation of fixed and anti-activation areas within the garment. --- ## User Interface and Unit Settings This section summarizes user interface features and settings related to measurement units and shortcuts. - Users can set measurement units to millimeters or inches in the settings. - Interface supports shortcut keys for efficient operation.
